title: Software Bill of Materials
summary: A software bill of materials is a machine-readable inventory of the components that make up a piece of software, typically listing each package with its name, version, supplier, unique identifier and the relationships that describe how components nest. The two dominant interchange formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, both of which support integrity hashes and licence metadata, and both of which can be produced per build or per released artifact. The operational purpose is rapid answerability: when a critical vulnerability or a compromised package is disclosed, an organisation that holds accurate SBOMs can determine exposure in minutes by querying inventories rather than by rebuilding and reviewing manifests by hand. That is also why SBOM accuracy, completeness and freshness matter far more than format choice. An SBOM generated once at a release and never regenerated drifts from reality as soon as a hotfix rebuilds a base image. For a practising engineer the practical problems are transitive completeness, identifier normalisation across ecosystems, correlating components to vulnerability data with trustworthy package identifiers, and handling the volume of inventory data without turning it into an unreadable dump. Useful programmes generate SBOMs automatically in the build pipeline, store them alongside the artifact they describe, sign them so their provenance can be checked, and test the whole path with a tabletop exercise that asks how fast the organisation could answer a specific exposure question. Formats without ingestion tooling or a query surface produce compliance artefacts that nobody can use during an incident.
objectives: You will be able to explain what an SBOM must contain to be useful during a vulnerability response, beyond a flat list of package names.
You will be able to compare SPDX and CycloneDX at a level sufficient to choose one for a given toolchain.
You will be able to describe how SBOMs are generated in a build pipeline and why they must be regenerated for every artifact build.
You will be able to design a query workflow that answers exposure questions against stored inventories quickly.
You will be able to explain why signing and provenance attestation of SBOMs matter for supply-chain assurance.
You will be able to evaluate an SBOM programme by running an exposure question and measuring time to a trustworthy answer.

beginner.definition: A software bill of materials is a list of every part inside a piece of software. It names each package, its version, and who supplied it. Think of the ingredient list on a food packet. When a bad ingredient is announced, you check the list instead of guessing.
beginner.whyItMatters: Modern software is mostly other people's code. One popular library can sit inside hundreds of your applications. When that library is found to be unsafe, you need to know quickly where it is used. Without a list, teams spend days rebuilding and searching by hand. With one, you answer in minutes and patch the right systems first.
howItWorks: During every build, a tool reads your dependency files and lists each package.
It records the name, version, supplier, and a unique identifier for each part.
It also notes which packages contain other packages, so the tree is complete.
The finished list is saved next to the exact software build it describes.
When a problem is announced, you search all stored lists for that package.
The list should be rebuilt every time the software is rebuilt, or it drifts.
beginner.example: Imagine a school cafeteria that keeps a full ingredient list for every meal it serves. One morning a supplier recalls a batch of peanut butter. The kitchen checks its lists and finds the three meals that used it. Only those trays are removed. Without those lists, staff would have to open every freezer and read every label by hand. A software bill of materials is that ingredient list for your code.
takeaways: A software bill of materials lists the parts inside your software, like a food label.
Regenerate it for every build, or it will describe the wrong thing.
Store it so you can search it during an emergency, not in a drawer.

exercises.title: Software Bill of Materials - EASY
exercises.summary: Recall and recognition: definitions, one clear answer, single-step questions.

exercises.title: Software Bill of Materials - MEDIUM
exercises.summary: Application: read a short log or alert and choose the correct next step.

exercises.title: Software Bill of Materials - HARD
exercises.summary: Analysis: a multi-step scenario with distractors, evidence to weigh, and a reason to give.

exercises.title: Software Bill of Materials - EXTREMELY HARD
exercises.summary: Synthesis under pressure: incomplete evidence, competing priorities, and a decision you must defend.
